title: Night-shift nurses and medication errors
hunch: Why do night-shift nurses seem to make more medication errors near the end of a shift?
followup: I keep noticing it's the last two hours of a twelve-hour night. Maybe it's fatigue stacking up with the pressure of handover?
aside: While that runs: is circadian low the same thing as sleep debt?
hypothesis: Among nurses working 12-hour night shifts, medication administration errors are more frequent in the final two hours of the shift than in earlier hours, partly because accumulated fatigue coincides with handover workload.
refined: In nurses on 12-hour night shifts, medication administration error rates are higher in the final two hours than in the first ten, and this difference is partly explained by self-reported fatigue.

resources.population_access: Nurses at one teaching hospital, about 60 on night rota
resources.skills: Basic statistics in R; no qualitative training
resources.tools: Online survey software; hospital incident reports with permission

outcome: Ruled: insufficient evidence · review included 0 of 26 · draft provisional

title: Why cities feel faster at night
hunch: Why do cities feel faster at night, even when there's less traffic?
followup: Maybe it's the lights: fewer reference points, so motion feels quicker?
aside: Quick one while that runs: does darkness change how we judge distance?
hypothesis: Pedestrians walking at night overestimate the speed of passing vehicles compared with the same vehicles in daylight, because reduced peripheral reference points distort speed perception.
refined: Pedestrians overestimate passing vehicle speed more at night than in daylight, and the difference shrinks when peripheral lighting adds visual reference points.

title: Trusting confident wrong answers
hunch: Why do people trust a confident wrong answer over a hesitant right one?
followup: It feels like confidence works as a shortcut for competence, especially when people can't check.
aside: While that runs: is this the same as the Dunning-Kruger effect?
hypothesis: When listeners cannot verify an answer, they rate a confidently delivered incorrect answer as more credible than a hesitantly delivered correct one.
refined: When listeners cannot verify an answer, delivery confidence increases its rated credibility more than its correctness does.
